# Evidence: behavioural science behind outreach messages

Ratings: **Measured** (study or large dataset with a method), **Survey** (self reported, stated sample),
**Practice** (experienced practitioners, unmeasured), **Vendor** (a seller's own data), **Untraced** (no source
found, or the source does not say it). A replication note follows the rating where it changes the reading:
"replicated", "mixed", "failed", "unreplicated" (no attempt found). "(secondary)" means only a summary was read.

## Publication bias, the frame for everything else

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Nudges run by government units at scale average 1.4 points (8%), against 8.7 points (33.4%) in journals | DellaVigna and Linos 2022 | Measured |
| About 70% of that gap is selective publication with low power | DellaVigna and Linos 2022 | Measured |
| Nudge practitioners forecast the real effects almost perfectly; academics overestimate | DellaVigna and Linos 2022 | Measured |
| After correcting for publication bias, no overall evidence remains for nudges in the largest meta-analysis | Maier et al. 2022 | Measured; contested by Mertens et al. and others |

## Reciprocity

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| An unrequested Coke about doubled raffle ticket purchases | Regan 1971 | Measured (secondary); the claimed replication by Gueguen and Vallee could not be confirmed (likely Meineri, Dupre, Gueguen, Vallee 2017, a related reciprocity study) |
| A small gift in a charity letter raised donation frequency 17%, a large one 75%, at a profit | Falk 2007, ~10,000 letters | Measured (secondary) |
| A money incentive with a survey raises response odds 1.87 times | Edwards et al. 2009, Cochrane | Measured (secondary) |
| An incentive sent up front beats one promised on reply, OR 1.61 (unconditional against conditional, not against no incentive) | Edwards et al. 2009, Cochrane; comparator from citing studies | Measured (secondary); consistent with the 2002 BMJ review (1.71) |
| A useful, no strings gift before the ask is the reciprocity move for a cold message | This folder's reading of the above | Practice resting on Measured |
| A favour request added to an unexpected contact reduces how much it is appreciated | Liu et al. 2022, as reported in press | Untraced at source (press coverage only) |

## Commitment and sequential requests

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Agreeing to a small request raises compliance with a larger one | Freedman and Fraser 1966 | Measured; small in meta-analyses; direct replication: held in Ukraine, not Poland, in 2003; failed in both in 2013 |
| Foot in the door effect sizes are small (around r = .1 to .2) | Beaman 1983, Dillard 1984 via Burger 1999 and secondary summaries | Measured (secondary; exact figures not read) |
| "But you are free" about doubles compliance | Carpenter 2013 | Measured; failed in bias controlled re-analysis |
| BYAF: g = 0.44 over 52 studies, g = 0.11 (ns) in the 7 low risk of bias studies; expected discovery rate 6% | Fillon et al. 2023, preregistered | Measured |
| BYAF works best face to face | Fillon et al. 2023 | Measured |
| Door in the face raises saying yes, not doing it | Feeley, Anker, Aloe 2012 | Measured (secondary) |
| A "yes ladder" of small questions raises sales replies | Sales folklore | Untraced |

## Curiosity

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Curiosity arises from an information gap and peaks at a moderate gap | Loewenstein 1994 | Measured as a review of older experiments; not a messaging test |
| Question and forward-reference headlines did not raise reading intentions over plain headlines | KQED headline experiment | Measured (one study, sample not stated) |
| Question headlines were rated less credible | KQED headline experiment | Measured (one study) |
| Negative words, not curiosity, raised headline clicks across thousands of A/B tests | Robertson et al. 2023 | Measured (secondary) |
| A curiosity gap raises replies to a cold message | Copywriting practice | Untraced |

## Specificity

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Concrete language by service agents raised satisfaction and later purchases, controlling for 30+ factors | Packard and Berger 2021 | Measured (secondary); unreplicated independently |
| Concreteness works because it signals listening | Packard and Berger 2021 | Measured (lab mediation, secondary) |
| +9% satisfaction, +13% purchase intention | Into the Minds write-up of Packard and Berger | Untraced at source |

## Social proof

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| A "most guests reuse towels" card beat the standard environmental card | Goldstein, Cialdini, Griskevicius 2008 | Measured (secondary); mixed on replication |
| In German hotels (928 guests) the norm card was no better than the standard card; both beat no card | Bohner and Schluter 2014 | Measured |
| Only the general norm, not the "same room" norm, worked in a US resort | Schultz et al. 2008 | Measured (secondary) |
| A descriptive norm about bad behaviour gave the most theft: 7.92% vs 4.00% for the other three signs; injunctive sign 1.67% (2,655 visitors, 1,140 pieces of wood; no no-sign control; 7.92% vs 5.00% for the positive descriptive sign not significant) | Cialdini et al. 2006, read at source | Measured; one study |
| Telling below-average energy users the average made them use more, unless an approval cue was added | Schultz et al. 2007 | Measured (secondary) |
| Social proof is "the one Cialdini lever that replicates well" | `linkedin-messages/` | Overstated: best supported of the six, but field replications mixed |

## Authority

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| High credibility sources usually persuade more, with conditions where they do not | Pornpitakpan 2004 review | Measured (secondary) |
| Credentials in a first message read as a pitch | Practitioners in `linkedin-messages/` | Practice |

## Liking and similarity

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| A shared birthday, first name or fingerprint type raised compliance | Burger et al. 2004, 4 studies | Measured (secondary); no direct replication; a 2013 conceptual extension agrees |
| Similarity did not help when the shared feature was common | Burger et al. 2004 | Measured (secondary) |
| A sender name similar to the recipient's raised survey returns | Garner 2005 | Measured (secondary); figures inconsistent across write-ups; unreplicated |
| Asking more questions, especially follow-ups, raises liking; people do not predict it | Huang et al. 2017 | Measured (secondary); unreplicated independently; contested (Kluger and Malloy 2019 reanalysis; authors' reply 2019; corrected for minor errors) |
| Senders underestimate how much a surprise contact is appreciated; more so with distance | Liu, Rim, Min, Min 2022, preregistered | Measured (secondary); tested with friends, not sales |

## Scarcity

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Cookies from a nearly empty jar were rated more desirable | Worchel et al. 1975 | Measured (secondary) |
| Scarcity raises perceived value, r = .12, heterogeneous | Lynn 1991 meta-analysis, as cited | Measured (secondary) |
| Scarcity mindset studies: 4 of 20 replicated, 6 reversed | O'Donnell et al. 2021 | Measured (secondary); a different construct from sales scarcity |
| A deadline or "limited spots" lifts cold replies | Sales practice | Untraced |

## The "because" effect

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Small favour: no reason 60%, placebic 93%, real 94% | Langer et al. 1978, reconstructed table | Measured (secondary) |
| Large favour: no reason 24%, placebic 24%, real 42% | Langer et al. 1978, reconstructed table | Measured (secondary) |
| The placebic effect did not replicate; reason type mattered | Folkes 1985 | Measured (secondary) |
| "Always say because" lifts commercial responses | Sales and marketing blogs | Untraced (no commercial test found) |

## Name personalisation

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Name in subject line: opens +20%, leads +31%, unsubscribes -17% | Sahni, Wheeler, Chintagunta 2018 | Measured; not repeated for first names in one small 2023 test |
| A first name in the subject line did not lift opens or clicks (about 3,500 students); a surname did (about 3,700 local politicians, a separate sample) | Defau and Zauner 2023 | Measured (abstract; sample figures secondary); one study, narrow audiences |
| Personalisation works by attention, not information | Sahni et al. 2018 | Measured |

## Loss aversion and framing

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Prospect theory patterns replicate: 94% of items, 12 of 13 contrasts, 19 countries | Ruggeri et al. 2020 | Measured |
| Loss aversion at small stakes is contested | Gal and Rucker 2018; Zeif and Yechiam 2022 | Measured, contested by Mrkva et al. 2020 |
| Experts are less loss averse on attributes they know | Mrkva et al. 2020 | Measured (secondary) |
| Loss framed messages are not reliably more persuasive than gain framed ones | O'Keefe and Jensen meta-analyses | Measured (secondary) |
| "Cost of inaction" framing lifts B2B replies | Sales methodology | Practice; no test found |

## AI written text

| Claim | Source | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| Profiles suspected of being AI written are trusted less, but only when readers think some are and some are not | Jakesch et al. 2019, read in part | Measured; extended by later work |
| People cannot detect AI self-presentations and rely on wrong cues | Jakesch, Hancock, Naaman 2023, 4,600 people | Measured (secondary) |
| Without a label, readers do not suspect AI and judge the sender as warmly | Zhu and Molnar 2026, 1,300+ people | Measured (secondary) |
| A disclosed AI message makes the sender seem lazy and insincere | Zhu and Molnar 2026; Asymmetric Effect preprint (N = 1,022) | Measured (secondary; preprint not peer reviewed) |
| Generic phrasing is what triggers the suspicion on LinkedIn | This folder's reading of Jakesch 2019 and 2023 | Practice resting on Measured |

|---|---|---|
| Frequent LLM users detect AI text at 92.7% with about 3 to 4% false positives; nonexperts near chance | Russell, Karpinska, Iyyer 2025, ACL | Measured (articles, not DMs) |
| People suspected of using AI replies are judged more negatively | Hohenstein et al. 2023 | Measured |
| Receptive written disagreement is more persuasive and draws fewer attacks | Yeomans et al. 2020, OBHDP | Measured, peer reviewed |
| Labelling an emotion lowers amygdala response | Lieberman et al. 2007 | Measured, self-labelling of faces only; does not support the sales use |

| Unity moves people beyond liking | Cialdini 2016 | Untraced (no effect data) |
